transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, Doc, I'm here because... honestly, I just can't seem to stop moving. It’s hard to explain exactly, but it’s like I’ve got this motor running inside me all day long. Just constantly revving, you know? From the minute I open my eyes, it's just humming away, and it never really shuts off. 

And it's a real problem because if I have to sit still anywhere, I just can't do it. Like at church, for instance. I try to sit in the pew and just listen to the sermon, but after a few minutes, I start feeling completely trapped. I get this tight, awful feeling, and I just have to get up and walk to the back or go to the bathroom just to do something, anything, to keep moving. 

It was the exact same thing out there in your clinic waiting room just now. The lady up front told me to have a seat, and I think I made it about two minutes before I was up pacing around the chairs and looking at the posters on the walls. I just couldn't stay in the chair. And it's like that at home, too. I can't even sit through a whole meal or watch a TV show without feeling boxed in. I just feel trapped all the time if I'm not moving, and I always have to get up and find something to do. It's driving me crazy, just having this engine going all the time and not being able to just sit and relax like a normal person.

When you're sitting still and feel that urge to move, is it more like you physically can't control the urge to move, or is it more like you feel anxious or panicky about being trapped and need to escape that feeling?

Well, Doc, honestly... I don't rightly know how to split the two up, if I'm being completely honest with you. It's not like... I mean, I don't think I'm having a panic attack or nothing like that. I'm not scared of the chair, you know? But it’s just this... this massive build-up. 

Like, okay, say I'm sitting there, right? First, my leg usually starts bouncing. I don't even tell it to bounce, it just starts going a mile a minute all on its own. And then I realize it's bouncing, and I try to press my foot down flat on the floor to make it stop because I know it annoys people. But when I do that, the feeling just moves up into my chest and my arms, and it's like this pressure, this really tight, uncomfortable pressure, just building and building and building. 

So, is it my body doing it or my head? I really couldn't tell you. It’s just like my whole system is screaming at me that sitting still is the absolute wrong thing to be doing right at that exact second. And yeah, I guess I do feel trapped, but not like... not like a claustrophobia kind of trapped where I'm scared of the room shrinking or the doors locking. It's more like I'm trapped inside my own skin, if that makes any sense at all? Like my skin is just too tight and the only way to loosen it up is to get up and walk around. 

I remember a couple weeks ago, my sister made me sit down at her kitchen table to help her sort out some mail, and I swear to you, I lasted maybe five minutes before I felt that exact thing. My knee was going, my hands were tapping the table, and she’s telling me to just sit still, but all I could think was, "If I don't stand up right now, I'm gonna jump straight out of my own body." So I don't know if that's me physically not being able to control my muscles or me just mentally needing to escape that awful tight feeling. It's just... it's just all of it at once, all tangled up together, and I just know I gotta get up. I've never really thought about whether it's an anxious thing or a physical thing, it's just what happens every single time.
How long have you been experiencing this constant need to move and inability to sit still? Has it been going on your whole life, or did it start at some point?

Well, Doc, that's a good question, and honestly, if I really sit down and think about it... well, I mean, I guess I've always been a little antsy, you know? Never been the type to just sit around doing nothing. But this? This feeling like my skin is crawling and I'm gonna explode if I don't get up? That hasn't been forever. 

I can actually pinpoint it pretty well. It's been about... well, let's see, it was right around the time the weather started turning cold two years ago. Yeah, so maybe two years and two months, right around there. And the reason I know that is because that's when my uncle—he's the one who raised me mostly—he took a real bad turn with his health. He had this stroke, out of nowhere, just sitting in his favorite recliner watching the game, and boom. Next thing we know, he's in the hospital for weeks, and then he comes home and he can't do hardly anything for himself anymore. 

And, well, since I'm not working right now, it fell on me to step up. Which is fine, he's family, I'd do anything for him. But man, it was a lot all at once. Suddenly I'm the one having to make sure his meds are sorted, helping him get to the bathroom, keeping the house clean, running to the pharmacy, dealing with the insurance people on the phone—which is a whole other nightmare, let me tell you, they put you on hold for an hour and expect you to just sit there. 

And I think... I think that's when this motor inside me really got cranked up to high gear and the knob broke off. Because before that, if I got antsy, I'd just go outside and tinker with my truck or walk down to the corner store. But suddenly, I couldn't just leave whenever I wanted. I had to be there, in the house, on call basically. I had to sit by his bed while he slept just in case he woke up and needed something. And that's when it got unbearable. That's when I started feeling that tight pressure in my chest and my legs bouncing out of control. It’s like, the more I had to sit still and be responsible, the more my body just refused to cooperate. And it's just been like that ever since, every single day for the last two years and a couple of months. Just non-stop.

Before this started two years ago, were you someone who worried a lot or felt anxious about things in general? Or did the worrying and anxiety really only start around the same time as this restless feeling?

Well, Doc... no, not really. I mean, if I really think on it... no. I was never much of a worrier before all this happened. People actually used to tell me I was too laid back, if you can believe it, considering how I am right now. 

Like, back in the day, I'd just kind of take things as they come. I never finished high school, you know, left in the middle of eighth grade, so I always just worked with my hands, doing odd jobs, landscaping, fixing up cars, whatever paid cash. And if work dried up for a week or two, or if I was short on rent, it didn't keep me up at night. I didn't sit around chewing my fingernails about what might happen tomorrow. I just figured, well, something will turn up. Like my buddy Dave, he used to get all worked up about every little thing—if his truck made a funny noise, he'd be sweating bullets thinking the transmission was gonna drop right there on the highway. But me? I'd just turn the radio up louder and keep driving until it actually broke down. That was just my way. I didn't borrow trouble, as my uncle used to say.

So, no, I didn't have all this... this heavy worry and this buzzing feeling back then. It really wasn't until the stroke. Because suddenly, it wasn't just me I was looking out for, right? If my truck breaks down, who cares, I walk. But if I mess up his pills, or if I don't hear him calling out from the bedroom because I'm out in the yard messing with some tools... well, that's a whole different ballgame. That's serious. 

So yeah, the worrying really kicked off right exactly when this whole motor-running-in-my-chest thing started. Before that, I was just... I was just doing my thing, not stressing. But now it's like my brain and my body are just constantly waiting for something terrible to happen, and I can't shut it off. Like I was saying about your waiting room out there, I just sit down and my head starts going, and my legs start going, and it's like if I don't get up and pace, I'm gonna miss something or do something wrong. It's just exhausting, Doc, it really is, never having a minute of peace where I can just sit and be still like I used to.
How is your uncle doing now, two years later? Is he still living with you and still requiring that same level of care and attention from you?

Well, Doc, yeah... yeah, he’s still with me. Still in the same house. We actually... well, we had to move his bed downstairs into what used to be the dining room, because getting him up those narrow stairs was just a disaster waiting to happen. I mean, I remember this one time, maybe six months after he got back from the hospital, I was trying to help him up the steps and my foot slipped, and I swear my heart almost jumped straight out of my throat. So, yeah, the dining room is his bedroom now. 

And as for how he’s doing... I mean, he’s alive, right? But it’s not like he bounced back to how he was before the stroke. He still can’t really use his left arm or leg much at all. He just sits in his recliner—we actually had to get a new one, one of those mechanical lift chairs that kind of tips you forward on an angle? Because otherwise I was pulling my shoulder out trying to haul him up every single time he needed to use the bathroom. 

And the care... man, it’s just as much, if not more, if I’m being completely honest. Because now he gets frustrated, you know? He used to be this big, tough guy, worked his whole life, and now he has to ask me to get him a glass of water or pick up the TV remote if he drops it. So he gets cranky, and I get antsy, and we just kind of bounce off each other all day. I’m still doing all his meals, sorting all his meds... and they just changed his pills again, which means another half hour on the phone with the pharmacy where I'm just pacing circles in the kitchen while that awful hold music plays. 

So yeah, I’m still on duty basically twenty-four-seven. I don’t get a day off. If I need to go to the grocery store, I have to wait until my sister can come over and sit with him, and even then, I’m literally running through the aisles like my shoes are on fire because I just have this feeling he’s gonna need something the second I’m not there. So it hasn't let up one bit, Doc. Not one bit.

When you're sitting still and feeling that tight pressure building up in your chest and legs, are you also having racing thoughts or worries running through your mind at the same time? Or is it more like your body is just restless and revved up, even when your mind feels relatively calm?

Well, Doc, I... I really don't know if I can separate the two, if I'm being completely honest. I've never really stopped to think about what my brain is doing while my body is throwing a fit. 

Like, okay, take the other night for example. We're sitting in the living room, and my uncle is dozing off in his lift chair while one of his old Westerns is on the TV—he watches those same episodes of Gunsmoke over and over, I swear I know all the words by now. But anyway, I'm sitting on the edge of the couch, just trying to be quiet so I don't wake him up, right? And that's when it starts. That tight feeling in my chest, and my right heel just starts going. Tap, tap, tap on the floorboards, like a jackhammer. 

And you're asking if my mind is racing with worries right then? I... I don't think so? I mean, I don't think I'm sitting there sweating over the electric bill or what the insurance company is gonna say next. It’s not like my brain is flipping through some big list of bad things that could happen. I haven't really noticed any specific thoughts like that. 

It's more like... well, my mind definitely isn't calm, but that's just because my body is so loud, you know what I mean? How can your head be peaceful when your chest feels like a shaken-up can of soda that's about to pop? I don't think I'm actually worrying about anything in those exact moments. I'm just so hyper-focused on how incredibly bad I need to stand up. It's like my brain is just static, just this loud buzzing noise telling my legs to move, move, move. So I end up getting up and just pacing around the kitchen island, tracing the grout lines in the tile, not really thinking about a single thing other than just walking off that awful pressure. So, yeah, I'm not really sure what my thoughts are doing, because I'm not really thinking at all, just... just reacting to my body, I guess.

Have you been taking any new medications in the past two years, or have you had any other health problems besides helping your uncle—like thyroid issues, diabetes, or anything like that—that started around the same time this restless feeling began?

Well, Doc, pills? For me? No, no way. I mean, I don't take anything at all. Not even a Tylenol unless my head is just absolutely splitting open, and even then, half the time I just drink a big glass of tap water and try to walk it off. I mean, you see what I deal with every single day with my uncle's medications, right? It’s a nightmare. He’s got the blood thinners, the cholesterol stuff, the nerve pills... he has this giant plastic organizer thing with the days of the week, and it’s got little compartments for morning, noon, evening, and bedtime. It’s literally like a full-time job just popping those little plastic lids open and making sure he doesn't drop them in the carpet. So, honestly, the absolute last thing I want to do is start swallowing a bunch of pills myself. I haven't started taking anything new, or anything old for that matter. 

And as for other health problems... no, I really don't think so. You mentioned thyroid and diabetes? Nah, nothing like that. Honestly, I haven't even been to a regular doctor for myself in... man, I don't even know how long. Years. Probably since I had to get a physical for a landscaping job back in my twenties. I just don't really get sick. Like, my buddy Dave, he's always catching some weird bug or complaining about his blood sugar or his bad knee, but me? I'm basically a horse. I eat whatever's around, I keep moving... I mean, my body works totally fine. It's really just this... this engine inside my chest that won't shut off, like we were talking about. 

But no actual diseases or anything. I mean, if my thyroid was messed up, wouldn't I be tired and sluggish all the time? I'm the exact opposite of sluggish. I'm so wired most of the day I feel like I could power the living room lamp if you just plugged it straight into my ear. So, yeah, no diabetes, no thyroid, no new medications... just me and this crazy restless feeling.
Have you been drinking more alcohol than usual in the past two years, or using any other substances like marijuana, cocaine, or anything else to help you cope with the stress?

Well, Doc, it’s funny you ask that, because I know people always assume that when you’re stressed out of your mind, you just naturally hit the bottle, right? Like in those movies where the guy has a bad day and just pours himself this massive glass of whiskey. But for me? No. No, not at all. 

I mean, think about it—I’m on duty twenty-four-seven with my uncle. If I throw back a six-pack and pass out on the couch, what happens if he tries to get up to use the bathroom and takes a spill? I can’t be out cold, or even just, you know, buzzed and slow. I have to be ready to jump up the second he calls my name or drops his remote. And honestly, even before all this with him, alcohol just never really did it for me. It makes my head feel all fuzzy and heavy, and like I said, my body is always going a hundred miles an hour. It’s like trying to pour thick syrup into a race car engine—it just clashes, you know? I hate that feeling of being weighed down. 

And as for the other stuff... marijuana, cocaine? Man, no way. Absolutely not. First off, I wouldn't even know where to get anything like that even if I wanted it, which I don't. I barely leave the house! Like I told you, I’m literally sprinting through the grocery store aisles just trying to buy milk and bread before my sister has to leave. When am I gonna have time to go track down some guy selling drugs? 

Plus, if you think about it, with how fast my chest is always buzzing and how tight everything feels with this... this restless pressure thing... if I took something like cocaine that’s supposed to amp you up even more? Holy cow, Doc, I think my heart would just explode. I’d probably vibrate right through the floorboards into the basement. And weed? My buddy Dave—the guy with the bad knee I was telling you about—he smokes that stuff sometimes, and he just melts into his couch eating potato chips for three hours straight. I can’t even sit still for three minutes! I'd probably go crazy feeling trapped in my own body like that. 

So no, none of that. I don't touch any of it. I mean, I drink coffee, sure, maybe a pot or two a day just because it gives my hands something to do while I'm pacing the kitchen waiting on hold with the pharmacy, but that's just normal grocery store coffee, you know? No booze, no drugs, nothing like that to cope. Just me dealing with it on my own.

Besides this restless, tight feeling in your chest and the need to move around, do you experience other things like sudden waves of fear or panic, or do you find yourself worrying a lot about things that might go wrong—like with your uncle's health, or money, or other situations?

Well, Doc, panic? Like, out of nowhere? No, I don't think so. When you say panic, I picture those people in the movies who have to breathe into a brown paper bag, you know? Like they're hyperventilating and think the world is ending or the sky is falling. I don't get anything like that at all. 

And the worrying part... it's kind of exactly like I was saying before about my thoughts. I just don't sit around dwelling on stuff. Like with my uncle's health, right? He's old. He's got a bad ticker, he's got bad joints, things are gonna go wrong, that's just a fact of life. My sister, she's the worrier in the family. She'll call me up on a Tuesday afternoon and talk for forty-five minutes straight about, oh, what if his Medicare doesn't cover the repairs on his lift chair, or what if he tries to get up to get a glass of water while I'm in the bathroom and he breaks his hip? And she gets herself all worked up, practically crying on the phone, stressing over every little detail of what might happen next month or next year. 

But me? I'm usually just walking laps around the kitchen island while she's talking on speakerphone, just tapping my fingers on the counter, waiting for her to finish so I can go fix the squeaky hinge on the back screen door or go rake the gravel in the driveway. I don't actually feel that worry she has. It's like my brain just doesn't hold onto those kinds of thoughts long enough to actually get scared about them. If something happens, it happens, and I'll deal with it right then and there. I literally don't have the attention span to sit on the couch and stew on a bunch of what-ifs. 

It's the exact same deal with money. We don't have a lot of it, obviously. I haven't worked a real paycheck job since I had to move in here full-time to watch him, so we're just scraping by on his disability checks and whatever my sister chips in. But I don't lay in bed at night staring at the ceiling calculating pennies and sweating over the electric bill. I lay in bed staring at the ceiling because my legs feel like they're plugged into a wall socket and I feel like I need to go sprint down the street in the pitch black. 

So, yeah, it's never fear, and it's never really worrying about the future or money or what's gonna happen to him. I don't get those waves of panic. It's always just right now, this exact second, my chest is tight and my body is screaming at me to get up and move. That's really all it ever is.

When you're lying in bed at night and your legs feel like they're plugged into a wall socket, like you mentioned—are you also thinking about things you're worried might happen with your uncle the next day, or is it just your body feeling wired without any particular thoughts attached to it?

No, no, see, that's exactly what I'm trying to say. It's not... there's no thoughts attached to it at all. I'm not laying there thinking, "Oh man, what if Uncle Joe falls tomorrow?" or "What if the pharmacy shorts us on his pills?" I mean, my brain just doesn't do that whole worrying thing. It's practically empty of that kind of stuff. 

It is literally just my body. I'll be laying there, staring at the ceiling fan—I count the little ridges on the blades sometimes, or watch the shadows from the streetlamp, just to give my eyes something to do—and my legs, man, they just start... buzzing. Like a low-grade hum right deep down in the bones. And I'll try to just lay still, I really will. I'll grip the edge of the mattress and tell myself, "Just go to sleep, man, you gotta be up to make his oatmeal in three hours anyway," but then my knee just starts bouncing under the blanket on its own. And if I try to force the knee to stop, then my foot starts tapping against the footboard. And then that tight, coiled-up feeling in my chest just kicks into absolute overdrive. 

There's no worry. There's no picture in my head of something bad happening. It's just... energy. This crazy, trapped energy. It gets so bad I just have to throw the covers off and get up, because if I stay in that bed one more second, I feel like my skin is gonna crawl right off my muscles. Half the time I end up pacing the hallway at three in the morning, or I'll go down to the basement and reorganize my uncle's old toolbox for the fifth time this month. I'll just sit there sorting the Phillips head screws from the flatheads, or wiping down the wrenches, just because my hands and my body need to be doing *something*. So, yeah, no worrying at all. Just a body that absolutely refuses to power down, no matter how quiet my brain is.

In the two years since your uncle's stroke, have you had any serious illnesses yourself, high fevers, infections, head injuries, or anything like that—or has a doctor ever told you that you have any medical condition that might affect your nerves or how your body feels?

Well, sick? Me? No, no, definitely not. I mean, honestly, I haven't even had so much as a sniffle or a cold in... gosh, I don't even know how long. Probably years. It’s actually kind of a running joke with my sister, because she catches every little bug that goes around her office, and she’s always complaining about her sinuses or a sore throat or whatever, but me? Nothing. I always tell her I’m moving too fast for the germs to catch me! 

But seriously, no high fevers, no infections, nothing like that at all. If I ever did get a bad fever and actually had to stay in bed, I don't even know what I'd do, because like I said, I literally can't stay in bed for more than a few hours without my legs going crazy. I'd probably be the worst sick person in the world, just pacing the house with a thermometer in my mouth. 

And head injuries? I mean, sure, I’ll whack my head on the low beam down in the basement sometimes—especially when I’m down there pacing around in the middle of the night, or digging through the old cardboard boxes trying to find some random extension cord or a specific size wrench just to keep my hands busy—but it’s just a bump, you know? A little scrape, maybe a curse word or two, but never anything real. I've never blacked out, never had a concussion, never had to go to the emergency room or anything like that. 

And as for a doctor telling me I have some kind of nerve condition or something wrong with my body? Well, Doc, you're pretty much the only doctor I've really talked to about myself in a long, long time. I haven't been to a regular checkup or a physical since way before my uncle had his stroke. I mean, who has the time for that? Between keeping an eye on him, making sure his pills are sorted, doing the grocery runs like a madman, fixing the gutters, tightening every loose hinge in the house... I just don't have a spare second to go sit in a doctor's waiting room and flip through old magazines. 

So, yeah, as far as I know, and as far as any actual medical stuff goes, my body is totally fine. My heart works, my lungs work, I don't have any diseases or nerve damage or whatever. It's just this... this motor inside me that won't shut off. But no, to answer your question, no sicknesses, no injuries, no medical conditions. Just me being me.
Has a doctor ever done any blood tests or physical exams on you in the past two years—like checking your heart rate, blood pressure, or running any lab work—even if it was just for something minor?

Well, like I was just saying, Doc, I really haven't seen a doctor for myself at all since before Uncle Joe got sick. So, no, no blood tests, no physicals, nobody checking my blood pressure or listening to my heart or doing any kind of lab work. I mean, the last time I even had my blood pressure taken, I think it was at one of those little machines they have sitting near the pharmacy counter at the grocery store. You know the ones? Where you stick your arm in the cuff and hit the button and it squeezes the life out of your bicep? 

I did that once, maybe three years ago, just because I was waiting for them to fill a prescription and I couldn't stand just standing there doing nothing. I was pacing back and forth in front of the greeting card aisle, and the machine was just sitting there, so I figured, why not? But even then, I couldn't sit still long enough for it to finish the reading. The cuff started getting tight, and my foot started tapping, and before it even gave me the numbers, I had to pull my arm out and go walk down the cereal aisle because I just felt too trapped sitting in that little plastic chair. 

So, no, no real doctor has done any tests on me in at least two years, probably longer. I just don't have the time to go sit in a waiting room, fill out a bunch of paperwork on a clipboard, and wait for them to draw blood or whatever. And honestly, I don't even know what they'd test for. Like I said, I don't get sick, I don't have fevers or infections. My body feels perfectly fine, except for the fact that it just constantly wants to move. I don't think they have a blood test that shows why my legs want to sprint a marathon at three in the morning, you know? 

I take Uncle Joe to his appointments, obviously. We're at the clinic or the hospital it feels like every other week for his heart or his joints or his blood thinners. And I watch them do all the tests on him—the blood draws, the EKGs, checking his vitals—and I'm usually just standing in the corner of the exam room, shifting my weight from one foot to the other, messing with the zipper on my jacket, just waiting for them to be done so we can get out of there. The nurses sometimes look at me like I'm crazy because I'm practically doing laps around the little rolling stool while they're trying to take his pulse. But they've never offered to check mine, and I've never asked. So, yeah, no tests, no exams, nothing like that for me. Just keeping up with his stuff is more than enough medical stuff for one family.

You mentioned you drink a couple pots of coffee a day while pacing in the kitchen—when you're drinking that much coffee, do you notice the restless feeling gets even worse, or does it feel about the same whether you've had coffee that day or not?

You know, it’s funny you ask about the coffee, because my sister was just telling me the other day—she came over to drop off some groceries, and I was on my, I don't know, maybe my fifth or sixth mug of the morning, just walking circles around the kitchen island while Uncle Joe was watching his game shows in the living room. And she looks at me and says, "You know that stuff is gonna make you jump out of your skin, right?" But honestly? I don't think it makes a lick of difference. I really don't. 

I mean, whether I drink two whole pots of the cheap stuff—I usually get that huge red plastic tub of Folgers, because it's just easier and I go through it so fast—or if I don't have a single drop, that restless feeling, that buzzing in my legs and my chest, it’s exactly the same. It's just always there. Like, there was this one morning last month where we completely ran out, and I couldn't get to the store because the car battery was dead, so I didn't have any coffee at all until like three in the afternoon. And let me tell you, my legs were still doing the exact same tap dance under the table. I was still pacing the exact same worn-out path into the linoleum from the sink to the fridge and back again, just bouncing off the walls the exact same way I always do. 

So, yeah, it doesn't get worse with the coffee. I think I just drink it because it gives my hands something to do, you know? Like, the whole routine of it. Scooping the grounds, pouring the water, watching it drip... it's an activity. It takes up a few minutes. And then holding the warm mug, taking a sip, walking across the room, taking another sip, tapping my fingers on the ceramic... it's just a rhythm. A way to keep moving. 

But as far as the actual jittery, wired feeling inside my body? Nah, the coffee doesn't touch it. It doesn't make it worse, doesn't make it better. My motor is just running at top speed no matter what I put in the tank. I could probably drink a glass of warm milk and I'd still be doing laps around the kitchen table. So to answer your question, no, I haven't noticed it changing anything. It's just... it's just always exactly the same.

When you're deeply focused on something—like watching a movie you really enjoy, or working on fixing your truck—do you still get that same leg bouncing and chest tightness, or does it go away when your mind is occupied?

Well, see, that's the thing. You'd think if I was really into something, my body would just quiet down and let me focus, but... man, I wish it worked like that. It really doesn't. 

Like, if I'm out in the driveway working on my truck—and I love messing with that old Chevy, getting under the hood, trying to figure out why the alternator is whining or whatever—I'll be totally zeroed in on what I'm doing, but my body is still just going, going, going. I'll be tapping the wrench against the fender, or shifting from my left foot to my right foot, kicking the tires, just constantly moving. 

Or movies! Oh man, Uncle Joe loves putting on those old Westerns, the really long ones with John Wayne, and sometimes I actually really want to watch them with him. But I can't just sit there. I'll be staring right at the screen, totally following the plot, but I'll realize I've completely shredded a paper napkin into a hundred tiny little pieces, or I'm bouncing my heel so hard on the floorboards that the whole couch is vibrating and Uncle Joe is giving me the side-eye. 

It actually gets me in trouble sometimes, because people think I'm not paying attention or that I don't care, but I do! Like, take a serious situation. Even when I’m really trying to be respectful—like when we’re at the bank talking to the manager about Uncle Joe’s accounts, or at church, or even sitting right here talking to you—my leg is just bouncing a mile a minute. My fingers are constantly tapping the arm of the chair, or I’m digging in my pockets and finding a receipt or a zip-tie or whatever, and I’m just twisting something in my hands the whole time. 

I can't help it. It's like my brain is locked into the movie or the truck or the conversation, but my body just didn't get the memo that we're supposed to be sitting still. Uncle Joe used to smack my knee when we were in a waiting room or something, telling me to quit shaking the chairs, but I literally don't even realize I'm doing it half the time until somebody points it out. My hands and my legs just have a mind of their own. So, yeah, no matter how much my mind is occupied, the rest of me is still putting on a one-man tap dance. It never stops, Doc. Never.

When you're asleep at night, does your body still move around a lot—like do you wake up and find your sheets all tangled, or does your bed partner ever tell you that you're kicking or thrashing around while you're sleeping? Or does the restlessness pretty much stop once you actually fall asleep?

Well, I mean, I don't really know for sure what happens when I'm actually out cold, right? Because, well, I'm asleep. And I don't have a wife or a girlfriend or anybody sharing the mattress with me to, you know, complain about me kicking them or elbowing them in the ribs or whatever. It's just me in that little back bedroom. Uncle Joe's room is all the way down the hall, right next to the bathroom—we put him there because of his bad knees so he doesn't have to walk far in the middle of the night—so he definitely can't hear what I'm doing in my room.

My hands and my legs just have a mind of their own. So, yeah, no matter how much my mind is occupied, the rest of me is still putting on a one-man tap dance. It never stops, Doc. Never.

doctor.intent: Distinguish between Generalized Anxiety Disorder with prominent physical restlessness (F41.1) and Restless Legs Syndrome or other movement disorder (G25.3) by determining if the restlessness is primarily a motor/neurological phenomenon that occurs involuntarily and persistently, even during sleep or when the patient is not consciously aware of it, versus a symptom driven by underlying anxiety that the patient can sometimes control or suppress through conscious effort.
doctor.question: When you're asleep at night, does your body still move around a lot—like do you wake up and find your sheets all tangled, or does your bed partner ever tell you that you're kicking or thrashing around while you're sleeping? Or does the restlessness pretty much stop once you actually fall asleep?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about restlessness, thrashing, or moving around during sleep, which is likely exploring other conditions like Restless Legs Syndrome or sleep disorders. The symptom profile for ADHD does not include symptoms related to movements during sleep.

patient.answer:
Well, I mean, I don't really know for sure what happens when I'm actually out cold, right? Because, well, I'm asleep. And I don't have a wife or a girlfriend or anybody sharing the mattress with me to, you know, complain about me kicking them or elbowing them in the ribs or whatever. It's just me in that little back bedroom. Uncle Joe's room is all the way down the hall, right next to the bathroom—we put him there because of his bad knees so he doesn't have to walk far in the middle of the night—so he definitely can't hear what I'm doing in my room. 

But I will say, the bed is usually a total disaster zone by the time the sun comes up. I've got this old blue quilt, the heavy kind my mom made years and years ago, and I swear, half the time I wake up and it's completely kicked off the end of the bed onto the floor, or it's twisted around my ankles like a giant pretzel. And the fitted sheet? Forget about it. I have to remake the whole bed every single morning because the corners always pop off. I don't know if they just don't make those pockets deep enough on cheap sheets anymore, or if I'm just in there wrestling an invisible alligator all night. 

But see, the thing is, I don't know if I'm doing all that kicking and tangling when I'm *actually* asleep, or if it's just from the hours I spend tossing and turning trying to get my body to shut down so I *can* fall asleep. Because just laying down in the dark? That's a whole production for me. I'll lay there, and my legs will just be itching to get up and walk down the hall. So I'll flip over to my left side, then two minutes later I flip to my right side, then I roll on my stomach, kick one leg out from under the covers because I feel like I'm burning up, pull it back in because then my foot gets cold... I'm just constantly adjusting and flipping like a burger on a grill. 

So maybe that's what messes up the sheets so bad, just the trying to get to sleep part. But once I actually cross over and I'm snoring? I really couldn't tell you, Doc. Nobody's in there to watch me, and I've never woken myself up from kicking the wall or anything like that. So I really have no idea if the motor finally cuts off or if it just keeps idling all night long.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has involuntary movements (akathisia/restlessness from a neurological cause) versus anxiety-driven restlessness by asking about whether the restlessness improves with movement or if movement provides only temporary relief before the urge returns
doctor.question: When you get up and walk around or move your body—like pacing in the kitchen or working on your truck—does that actually make the tight feeling and the leg bouncing go away completely, or does it just feel better for a little while and then come right back as soon as you try to sit down again?

target_item.name: Leaving_Seat
target_item.manifestation: In meetings, meals, and waiting rooms, I keep standing up to get water, check outside, or move around, even when everybody else is sitting and looking at me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the inability to remain seated and whether the restless feeling returns upon sitting down, which directly probes the symptom of frequently leaving one's seat in situations where sitting is expected.

patient.answer:
Well, see, that's the whole problem right there. It never really goes away completely. It’s more like... I mean, when I’m up and pacing or out there wrenching on the truck, it feels better, sure, because the energy has somewhere to go, you know? I'm using it up. But the absolute second I try to sit down—bam. It’s right back. It’s like a rubber band snapping. And it makes it practically impossible to just... be normal in places where you're supposed to sit still. 

Like, take supper time with Uncle Joe. He likes to sit at the table, eat his meatloaf or whatever, and just have a quiet meal. A normal person just sits and eats. Not me. I'll take maybe two bites of potatoes, and then I just have to stand up. I’ll tell him I need to get a glass of water. So I get the water, sit back down. Two minutes later, I’m up again, walking over to the front window just to check outside, see if the neighbor's dog got loose or if a car drove by, which is ridiculous because we live on a dead-end street and nobody ever drives by. But I just have to get up and move around. 

And it's not just at home, either. It’s everywhere. If I have to go to a meeting, or like when we were in that waiting room at the Social Security office last month—man, that was a total nightmare. They make you take a number and just sit in those hard plastic chairs for hours. I couldn't do it. I sat down, stood up to go look at the bulletin board. Sat back down, stood up to go get a drink from the fountain. Sat back down, stood up to pace by the door. 

And the whole time, everybody else in the room is just sitting there, totally still, reading magazines or looking at their phones, and they’re all just staring at me. I can see them out of the corner of my eye, giving me these looks like, "What on earth is wrong with this guy?" Even the security guard was watching me like I was about to cause trouble or something. 

But I can't help it! The tightness in my chest and that buzzing in my legs just builds and builds if I try to force myself to stay in the seat. It gets so uncomfortable I feel like I'm gonna explode if I don't stand up right that second. So, yeah, the pacing helps for a minute, but the relief only lasts exactly as long as I'm on my feet. Once I sit, the clock resets, and I'm just looking for the very next excuse to jump out of my chair again.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the restlessness is primarily a movement disorder (akathisia from G25.3) that is independent of anxiety, or whether it is driven by underlying anxiety (F41.1). Specifically, I need to clarify if the patient experiences the urge to move even when he is mentally calm and not worried about anything, which would suggest akathisia rather than anxiety-driven restlessness.
doctor.question: Let me ask you this: are there times during the day when your mind feels completely relaxed and at peace—like you're not thinking about your uncle, not worried about anything at all, just genuinely calm in your head—but your body still has that urge to move and that tight feeling in your chest anyway?

target_item.name: Feeling_Restless
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I feel like I got a motor running inside me all day, and if I have to sit still at church, at the clinic, or at home, I feel trapped and have to get up or do something.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the internal, subjective feeling of restlessness (the urge to move and tight feeling in the chest) even when the mind is calm, which corresponds to the symptom of feeling restless.

patient.answer:
Well, honestly Doc, that right there... that’s the whole reason I finally came in to see you in the first place. Because, yeah, even if my head is totally quiet—which, you know, doesn't happen every single day, but sometimes I'm just sitting on the front porch, sun is shining, I'm not worried about Uncle Joe or money or anything at all, just totally at peace—my body still acts like it's getting ready to run a footrace. 

It’s like... I feel like I got a motor running inside me all day long, just humming away. It doesn't care if my mind is relaxed or not. That motor is just always on. And if I have to sit still anywhere—like, say we go to church on Sunday, and I'm feeling real peaceful listening to the choir, or even right now sitting here in the clinic with you, or just trying to relax in my own recliner at home—if I have to just sit there, I start feeling completely trapped. 

It’s not an anxious thought in my head, it’s a physical thing. I feel trapped in the chair, trapped in my own skin, and this pressure just builds and builds until I absolutely have to get up or do something. I just have to. I'll be sitting there telling myself, "Everything is fine, just sit here, enjoy the quiet," but the motor is just going and going, and my chest gets tight, and my legs start itching, and before I even know what I'm doing, I'm on my feet again looking for a wrench or a broom or something to mess with. So yeah, peaceful mind or not, the engine never actually cuts off. It just keeps idling high, making me feel like a caged animal if I don't get up and move.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the restlessness is primarily a physical sensation (akathisia - a movement disorder) versus primarily anxiety-driven, by asking about the temporal relationship between the urge to move and any conscious awareness of discomfort or the need to escape it.
doctor.question: When you get that urge to move and stand up—do you feel the physical discomfort or tightness first and then decide you need to move, or do you find yourself already standing up before you even realize you felt uncomfortable?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking a clarifying question about the sequence of feeling physical discomfort versus the action of standing up, likely to differentiate between akathisia and ADHD impulsivity/hyperactivity. This does not map to a new symptom in the provided profile.

patient.answer:
Man, that’s... that’s a real chicken-or-the-egg kind of question right there, Doc. I mean, I honestly don't know for sure. Because it’s not like I’m sitting there having a debate with myself, right? It’s not like I sit there and think, "Oh, my chest is getting tight, my legs are buzzing, I better stand up now." It doesn't work like that. 

It's more like... well, take the other night. Uncle Joe was watching his baseball game. He loves baseball, watches every single inning, which just drives me up the wall because it's so slow, but I try to sit in the living room to keep him company, you know? I'm in the brown recliner—the one with the duct tape on the armrest where the foam was falling out—and I'm just sitting there. And the next thing I know, I'm standing right in front of the TV set. 

I didn't decide to get up. I just... was up. I was standing there messing with the volume knob on the digital box, or picking up a piece of lint off the carpet. And Uncle Joe is hollering, "Hey, you make a better door than a window!" and I'm just standing there blinking, trying to figure out why I even got out of the chair in the first place. 

So, did the tightness make me move? I mean, the tightness is always there, kind of humming in the background, but I definitely don't realize it's gotten bad until I'm already on my feet pacing the rug. It’s like my legs just completely bypass my brain. They just go, "Alright, we're done sitting," and they launch me up before I even have a second to realize I'm uncomfortable. So I really couldn't tell you what triggers what, because there's no actual decision being made. I just find myself halfway to the kitchen before I even realize I left the living room.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient's movements are involuntary (akathisia/restless legs syndrome) or primarily anxiety-driven by asking if he can physically prevent the movements when he tries hard to do so
doctor.question: When you're sitting down and your leg starts bouncing or you feel that urge to move—if you really concentrate and try your absolute hardest to keep your leg completely still and not let it bounce, can you actually do that, or does it just keep moving no matter how hard you try to stop it?

target_item.name: Fidgeting
target_item.manifestation: Even when I’m trying to be respectful, my leg is bouncing, my fingers are tapping the chair, or I’m twisting something in my hands the whole time.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about my ability to control my leg bouncing and the urge to move while seated, which directly relates to my symptom of fidgeting with my hands or feet.

patient.answer:
Doc, I swear to you, I try. I mean, I really, really try. It ain't like I don't know how it looks to other people. Like, take a couple weeks ago when Reverend Thomas came by the house to check on Uncle Joe. Now, I know you gotta be respectful around the Reverend, right? He's an older fella, very proper, wears a suit even when it's ninety degrees outside. So I tell myself before he even knocks on the door, 'Just sit down, keep still, act right.' 

And I sit there on the good sofa—the floral one we usually keep the plastic cover on—and I just stare at my knee. I tell my leg, 'Do not move.' But it’s like... it’s like trying to hold back a river with a screen door. 

Even when I am trying my absolute hardest to be respectful and just listen to the man talk, my leg is bouncing away, going a mile a minute. And if I somehow manage to mash my foot down hard into the rug and force that leg to stay put, well, the energy just shoots right up my arms instead. Next thing I know, my fingers are tapping on the wooden arm of the chair, just rat-a-tat-tat, or I’ll realize I’m twisting something in my hands the whole entire time. Like a paper napkin, or a piece of loose thread I pulled off the cushion, or I'm just wringing my own knuckles together until they pop. 

And Uncle Joe will give me this look, you know, clearing his throat real loud like I'm doing it on purpose to be rude to the Reverend. But I'm not! I'm putting every single ounce of brainpower I have into just sitting there like a normal person. But if I stop the leg, the hands start. If I sit on my hands, my feet start tapping. It just leaks out of me no matter what. So no, I can't just concentrate and make it stop. I might be able to freeze my leg for about ten seconds, but then I'm not even hearing a word anybody is saying because my whole brain is just screaming at my leg to stay down, and by then my fingers are already drumming on the coffee table anyway.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the restlessness and involuntary movements are primarily a neurological/motor phenomenon (akathisia from antipsychotics or other causes) versus an anxiety disorder, by asking if the patient has ever taken antipsychotic medications or other psychiatric drugs that could cause akathisia as a side effect.
doctor.question: Have you ever been prescribed any psychiatric medications in the past—like antipsychotics, antidepressants, or anti-anxiety pills—even if it was just for a short time, or have you ever taken any medication that a doctor said was for your nerves or mood?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about past psychiatric medication history, which is not covered by any of the items in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, no, Doc, I ain't never taken nothing like that. Not a single one of those... well, whatever it is you just called them. Anti-somethings. Never had them. Truth be told, I ain't much of a doctor-going kind of guy anyway, present company excluded, of course. I mean, Uncle Joe, he has his blood pressure pills and his water pills and a whole little plastic box with the days of the week stamped on the lids, but me? Nah. 

The only time I ever really went to the clinic before all this was maybe... shoot, it must have been five or six years ago. I was helping my buddy fix the transmission on his old Ford truck, and the jack slipped and I busted my hand up real good. Smashed two fingers right against the concrete, turned completely purple. They gave me some kind of pill for the swelling, ibuprofen or something like that, but never anything for my nerves or my mood. 

Uncle Joe, he is always saying that those nerve pills just turn a man into a zombie anyway. He had a neighbor once, old Mrs. Gable, who took something for her nerves and he told me she just sat on her porch all day staring at the grass grow, not even blinking when the mailman walked by. So I never messed with any of that. I never saw a doctor for my head before, never got a prescription for my mood, never took a pill to calm down or anything like that. I have just been dealing with this whole thing all on my own for my whole life. Just dealing with it the best I can, you know? So no, no psychiatric pills or nerve pills or whatever they are called. Never touched them, never been prescribed them, not even for a single day.

inference.note: F41.1 ruled out. Patient denies experiencing panic attacks, racing thoughts, or worry-based anxiety. Restlessness is purely motor/physical with no cognitive component. Symptoms are NOT triggered by worry but rather occur independently. Patient explicitly states peaceful mind but body still has motor running. This is akathisia (G25.3) - a movement disorder characterized by subjective inner restlessness and objective inability to remain still, NOT generalized anxiety disorder. Two-year timeline following stressor, constant physical restlessness independent of anxiety, inability to suppress movement despite conscious effort, and lack of anxiety/panic symptoms all support akathisia diagnosis.

opening_question.question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a two-year history of persistent restlessness, inability to sit still, involuntary leg bouncing, and internal pressure/tightness that is primarily motor-driven rather than anxiety-driven. The symptoms began acutely following his uncle's stroke and associated caregiver stress, but the patient explicitly denies racing thoughts, worry, panic attacks, or anticipatory anxiety. When directly asked whether his mind is calm while his body is restless, he confirms this dissociation. His symptoms persist regardless of caffeine intake, cognitive engagement, or mental state. The motor restlessness cannot be voluntarily suppressed despite significant effort. The phenomenology—involuntary movements, inability to inhibit motion, physical compulsion to move—is most consistent with Akathisia (G25.3), a movement disorder characterized by subjective restlessness and inability to remain still, which can occur secondarily to stress or other triggers. The absence of true generalized anxiety symptoms, panic, and the purely motor/physical nature of the presentation argues against primary anxiety disorder.
